posts.text:
🌏 ASEAN carbon credits will go further with one shared "methodology"
Having recently drafted a new GHG methodology for a Japanese client to submit to Thailand’s organization, I have seen firsthand how crucial standardization is. When bringing international practices into local frameworks, the biggest hurdle is aligning the rules.
That is why the ASEAN Common Carbon Framework (ACCF) among carbon market associations in Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore is a big deal. Its aim is simple. A credit issued in one country should be tradable in another.
When people talk about standardized methodologies, they often think of solar. Yet much of our region's emissions sit in agriculture, livestock, and waste, where countries calculate very differently.
🌾 Rice alternate wetting and drying
🐄 Livestock feed and manure management
♻️ Biogas from organic waste
🌿 Biochar
From a consulting perspective, the same standard does not mean the same numbers. Equation structures and MRV principles should match, while parameter values must reflect local breeds, diets, climate, and waste systems.
When this happens, buyers can compare credits easily, and developers do not restart from zero in every country. Note that ACCF is an industry pact, so it doesn't bind any government yet.
Which sector needs a shared standard first?
#CarbonCredits #ASEAN #MRV #PremiumTVER #GreenFintech

posts.text:
Double Counting: When One Ton Is Sold Twice

Critiques of carbon projects in Indonesia have highlighted the persistent risk of double counting—occurring when projects are developed without government approval and overlap with national NDC accounting. In some cases, private-to-private offset trades have resulted in climate benefits being counted twice, because private sellers are not obligated to increase mitigation ambition as compensation for transferred offsets.

This is not a technical footnote. It strikes at the heart of carbon market credibility. If a single ton of emission reduction can be sold twice, then what the market is trading is not climate benefit—it is accounting fiction. And accounting fiction does not lower atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases.

The integrity of verification systems depends entirely on their ability to prevent this. Yet the gaps remain open, often because regulatory oversight is incomplete, incentives favor volume over rigor, and enforcement is weak across jurisdictions.

For every corporate buyer and project developer, the question is uncomfortable but necessary: how robust is the integrity of the system you are participating in? If double counting remains possible, then the "verified" label may be offering comfort rather than certainty.

The credibility of the entire voluntary market rests on closing these gaps—not eventually, but now.

#DoubleCounting #CarbonIntegrity #Article6 #ParisAgreement #CarbonMarkets #MRV

Bengaluru-based AI lab FrontiersMind has launched NandiBERT, a family of open-source AI models designed to understand and process text across 17 languages, including 13 Indian languages, English, Bahasa Indonesia, Malay and Arabic.

Unlike a chatbot that generates conversations, NandiBERT is an encoder model. It helps AI applications understand written information, identify relevant content, classify documents and retrieve information more accurately.

The model comes in two versions: 150 million and 450 million parameters, supporting up to 16,000 and 32,000 tokens respectively.

According to FrontiersMind's published benchmarks, NandiBERT-450M outperformed the previous leading Indic model across all seven evaluated Indian-language tasks. The smaller 150M version also achieved a higher average score than a competing model with nearly twice as many parameters.

Its performance extends to English. Across ten classification and retrieval benchmarks, both versions achieved higher average scores than comparable ModernBERT and Ettin models in the company's evaluations.

NandiBERT's model weights are openly available under the Apache 2.0 licence, allowing developers and businesses to access, adapt and use them commercially.

The published results demonstrate promising multilingual capabilities, with real-world performance depending on how the models are adapted and deployed.

CHINA WANTED ACCESS TO NVIDIA'S AI CHIPS. THE SPY SCANDAL MAY HAVE MADE THAT EVEN HARDER.

The controversy surrounding Jensen Huang has opened a new front in the technology battle between Washington and Beijing. And the consequences for China could be considerably more damaging than initially expected.

The allegations involving Huang and Alice Huang, a Singapore-based business executive suspected by US authorities of having links to Chinese intelligence, have brought renewed attention to the movement of advanced American chips into China. Beijing denies the espionage allegations. They have not been independently established.

But Washington is responding with measures that extend well beyond the individuals involved.

Singapore-based Megaspeed has been blacklisted by the US Commerce Department. Additional restrictions now require export licenses for certain advanced AI chips shipped to several Southeast Asian countries, including Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia. These measures target routes that US officials believe could be used to divert restricted technology into China.

The commercial consequences are already becoming visible. Some Chinese customers have cancelled or delayed NVIDIA orders amid uncertainty over which products they will still be allowed to buy.

NVIDIA has also decided to stop selling even certain chips that had previously been permitted for export to China, including the H20 and H200.

For Beijing, this creates an uncomfortable situation. Chinese technology companies still want access to NVIDIA's processors and software. Yet the political climate in Washington is moving toward tighter scrutiny, not greater access.

There is another consequence. Every new restriction gives China's semiconductor industry another reason to accelerate its efforts to develop domestic alternatives. Companies such as Huawei are already working to close the gap, backed by substantial state support and a huge domestic market.

That will not happen overnight. NVIDIA retains significant advantages in chip performance, software and its developer ecosystem. Replacing that combination is a formidable undertaking.

But Washington should consider the longer-term consequences of its strategy. Restricting access to American technology can slow a competitor's progress in the short term. It can also give that competitor a powerful incentive to eliminate its dependence on American suppliers.

The immediate loser may be China's access to NVIDIA chips. The longer-term beneficiary could be China's own semiconductor industry.

And that is the strategic calculation Washington cannot afford to ignore.
